q: Why can't an interrupt handler sleep or do heavy work?
a: It runs with interrupts (at least on that line/core) blocked and outside any process context; sleeping would freeze that core's interrupt handling. Heavy work goes to a bottom half.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: What does NAPI do and why?
a: After the first interrupt it disables the NIC's interrupt and polls batches of packets until the queue is empty, avoiding an interrupt storm at high packet rates.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: How does Linux know which driver to load for a newly plugged device?
a: The bus reads the device IDs, the kernel emits a uevent with a modalias, udev matches it to a module and runs modprobe; the driver's probe() then claims the device.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: A node shows one core at 100% in si while others are idle. What do you check?
a: /proc/interrupts: NIC queue IRQs probably land on one core. Add queues / RSS, fix IRQ affinity or enable irqbalance, consider RPS.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why must GPU drivers be installed on the node and not just in the container?
a: Drivers are kernel code. Containers share the host kernel; they only carry user-space libraries that talk to the host's driver.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: If USB devices can't speak first, how does a key press reach the computer?
a: The host polls the keyboard's interrupt endpoint every 1–8 ms; the next poll after the press returns a report instead of NAK.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why does one generic driver work for almost every keyboard and mouse?
a: HID devices describe their report layout in a report descriptor, so the HID core can parse any of them.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Does the keyboard send the letter 'a'?
a: No. It sends usage 0x04, a key position. The layout (xkb in user space) decides it means "a", "q" or something else.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: How much latency can a 125 Hz polling rate add?
a: Up to 8 ms (average ~4 ms) before the host even sees the report.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why do some hardened servers block unknown USB devices?
a: A device can claim to be a keyboard and type commands (BadUSB). Allow-listing with USBGuard prevents that.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Where does the letter (as opposed to the key position) get decided on a Wayland desktop?
a: In the application, by xkbcommon applying the keymap the compositor sent, using the current modifier state.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why are /dev/input/event files not readable by normal users?
a: Reading them would let any program capture every keystroke system-wide (a keylogger).

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why could any X11 app capture your passwords, but not on Wayland?
a: X11 let any client listen to all input; on Wayland the compositor only sends input to the focused surface.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: A game should use WASD on every layout. Which KeyboardEvent field should it read?
a: event.code, the physical key position, not event.key.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Who generates key repeat when you hold a key down?
a: The client/toolkit, using the rate and delay advertised by the compositor; the keyboard only reports that the key is still down.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
page: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: If you switch from QWERTY to AZERTY, does the code sent over USB change for the same physical key?
a: No. The code (0x04) describes the key's position. Translating it to a character is done by the OS or the app, using the layout.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
page: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: With 8 ms polling, how long can a keypress wait in the worst case?
a: About 8 ms. If you press right after a poll, the report waits until the next one.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
page: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: What happens to the program the CPU was running when the interrupt arrived?
a: The CPU finishes the current instruction, saves the program's state (RIP, RFLAGS, …) on the stack, runs the handler, and resumes the program exactly where it was with iretq. The program never notices.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
page: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why don't applications read the keyboard directly from /dev/input?
a: Security and focus. If every app could read every key, every app would be a keylogger. The compositor only delivers events to the focused window.

chTitle: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
page: Chapter 1 — What happens when you press “A”?
q: Why is the 'A' keycode 38 on X11 but 30 on Wayland?
a: For historical reasons X11 adds 8 to the evdev code (30 + 8 = 38). Wayland sends the evdev code as is.

q: Why does an amd64 image fail on a Graviton node?
a: Graviton is ARM64; the binary's instructions belong to a different ISA. The kernel refuses to execute it (exec format error).

q: Why is decoding x86 harder than ARM64?
a: x86 instructions are 1–15 bytes long, so the CPU must find instruction boundaries first; ARM64 instructions are always 4 bytes.

q: In a gdb session a function crashed. Where do you find its first two arguments?
a: In RDI and RSI (System V calling convention), if they haven't been overwritten yet.

q: A program dies with SIGILL after migrating to another VM type. What's a likely cause?
a: It was compiled for CPU extensions (AVX-512, AVX2) the new CPU doesn't support.

q: What does xor eax, eax do and why do compilers prefer it?
a: Sets EAX to zero; it's shorter than mov eax, 0 and recognized by the CPU as a dependency-breaking zero idiom.

q: Why does reading one byte from RAM cost as much as reading 64?
a: Memory moves in 64-byte cache lines; the whole line is fetched either way.

q: Why is iterating a linked list much slower than an array of the same length?
a: Each node can be anywhere in memory, so each step can be a cache miss and the prefetcher can't predict the next address.

q: Two threads increment two different counters and get slower than one thread. Why?
a: The counters share a cache line (false sharing); each write invalidates the other core's copy.

q: What does NUMA mean for a database on a 2-socket server?
a: Memory attached to the other socket is slower; threads and their data should stay on the same node (or memory interleaved).

q: Why do huge pages help large heaps?
a: One TLB entry covers 2 MB (or 1 GB) instead of 4 KB, so far fewer TLB misses and page-table walks.

q: How can a CPU finish one instruction per cycle if each takes 15+ cycles?
a: Pipelining: many instructions are in different stages at the same time.

q: Why does sorting an array make a branchy loop over it faster?
a: The if becomes predictable (all false, then all true), so mispredictions and pipeline flushes nearly disappear.

q: What does Spectre exploit?
a: Speculative execution leaves traces in the cache that aren't rolled back; timing cache accesses reveals data read speculatively.

q: Your cloud VM has 8 vCPUs. How many physical cores is that likely to be?
a: Usually 4 physical cores with SMT (2 hardware threads each), depending on the provider and instance type.

q: A pod with low average CPU shows latency spikes and rising cfs_throttled_periods. What's happening?
a: Its threads use up the CPU limit's quota early in each 100 ms period and are throttled until the next one. Raise or remove the limit, or reduce thread bursts.

q: Why is iterating over an array faster than over a linked list with the same number of elements?
a: The array's elements sit next to each other, so one 64-byte cache line brings several of them at once and the prefetcher can guess what comes next. Linked-list nodes are scattered, so each one may need a ~100 ns trip to RAM.

q: What does the RIP register hold, and who changes it?
a: The address of the next instruction. It normally advances by the instruction's length. Jumps, call, ret and interrupts change it directly.

q: What does ret actually do?
a: It pops the return address that call pushed onto the stack and puts it into RIP, so execution continues right after the call.

q: Why can a program compiled with GCC call a library compiled with Clang?
a: Both follow the same calling convention (System V ABI): which registers carry arguments and return values, and which registers each side must preserve.

q: Roughly how many CPU cycles does one RAM access cost at 3 GHz?
a: About 300 cycles (~100 ns × 3 cycles/ns). During that time the core could have executed hundreds of instructions.

q: Why is fork() fast even for a process with gigabytes of memory?
a: Copy-on-write: parent and child share pages until one of them writes; only page tables are copied up front.

q: What's the difference between a zombie and an orphan?
a: A zombie has exited but hasn't been reaped by its parent. An orphan is still running but its parent died; it gets adopted by PID 1.

q: Your pod always takes 30 s to stop. Why?
a: The app (PID 1) doesn't handle SIGTERM, so nothing happens until the kubelet sends SIGKILL after the grace period.

q: What does exit code 137 mean?
a: 128 + 9: the process was killed by SIGKILL, commonly by the OOM killer or after the termination grace period.

q: When would you use processes instead of threads?
a: When you need isolation (a crash or memory leak shouldn't take everything down) or to avoid a lock like Python's GIL.

q: What happens to a task that calls read() on a socket with no data?
a: It blocks: leaves the run queue and sleeps until data arrives; the scheduler runs something else.

q: Load average is 16 on a 16-core server but CPU is 20%. What's going on?
a: Load includes D-state tasks; many tasks are probably stuck in uninterruptible I/O (disk, NFS).

q: What's the difference between a CPU request and a CPU limit in Kubernetes?
a: Request sets cpu.weight (share under contention, used for scheduling); limit sets cpu.max (hard quota, causes throttling).

q: Why can a CPU limit hurt latency even when average CPU usage is well below it?
a: Multiple threads can burn the whole period's quota early, then the container is throttled for the rest of the period.

q: Why should runtimes like the JVM or Go know the container's CPU limit?
a: They size thread pools and GC workers from the number of CPUs; seeing 64 host cores with a 2-CPU limit causes heavy throttling.

q: A process allocates 4 GB but RSS is only 50 MB. Is something wrong?
a: No. Pages are only backed by RAM when touched (demand paging); untouched allocations cost nothing.

q: free shows 1 GB free on a 64 GB server. Should you worry?
a: Look at available. Most RAM is probably page cache, which the kernel drops when applications need memory.

q: What's the difference between a minor and a major page fault?
a: Minor: the data is already in RAM, only a mapping is added. Major: the data must be read from disk.

q: Why did my JVM pod get OOMKilled even though -Xmx is below the limit?
a: The JVM uses memory outside the heap (metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, JIT code, native libs); heap + all that exceeded memory.max.

q: Why can't Kubernetes throttle memory the way it throttles CPU?
a: CPU time can be delayed; memory already in use can't be taken back without reclaiming (cache/swap) or killing the process.

q: What happens between calling read() and the kernel running its code?
a: libc sets the syscall number and args in registers and executes syscall; the CPU switches to ring 0 and jumps to the kernel entry, which dispatches to the read handler.

q: write() returned success. Is the data on disk?
a: Not necessarily: it's in the page cache as a dirty page. Only after fsync() (or writeback) is it on stable storage.

q: How does nginx handle 50,000 connections with a few worker processes?
a: Non-blocking sockets + epoll: each worker waits for readiness on all its sockets and only handles the ready ones.

q: You deleted a 20 GB log but the disk is still full. Why?
a: A process still has the file open; the inode isn't freed until the last fd is closed. Restart/reload the process or truncate via /proc/PID/fd.

q: Why can /dev/shm usage cause an OOMKill in a pod?
a: It's tmpfs, i.e. RAM, and counts against the container's memory cgroup.

q: Is a container a lightweight VM?
a: No. It's a regular process on the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups. A VM runs its own kernel.

q: Why can two containers in the same pod reach each other on localhost?
a: They share one network namespace (held by the pause container).

q: Which kernel feature enforces a memory limit, and what happens when it's exceeded?
a: The memory cgroup (memory.max); the OOM killer kills a process inside that cgroup.

q: Why is privileged: true dangerous?
a: It gives all capabilities, disables seccomp/AppArmor confinement and exposes host devices; the container can usually control the host.

q: An app inside a container reads /proc/meminfo and sees 256 GB on a 2 GB limit. Why?
a: /proc/meminfo isn't namespaced; the app must read the cgroup files (memory.max) to learn its real limit.

q: Two threads of the same process and two separate processes both run in parallel. What is the key difference?
a: Threads share one address space (memory, open files) and can read each other's data directly. Separate processes have separate page tables and cannot see each other's memory without explicit sharing (pipes, sockets, shared memory).

q: Why can't a buggy process overwrite another process's memory?
a: Each process has its own page table. Its virtual addresses can only map to the physical frames the kernel gave it, and the MMU enforces this on every access.

q: What happens, step by step, when your program calls write()?
a: libc puts the syscall number in RAX and arguments in RDI/RSI/RDX, executes syscall, the CPU switches to ring 0, the kernel's VFS finds what fd refers to and calls the right driver, the result comes back in RAX, and the CPU returns to ring 3.

q: A container keeps getting killed with OOMKilled. Which kernel mechanism is doing it?
a: The memory cgroup limit plus the kernel's OOM killer. The container used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed a process inside it.

q: Why should your container's PID 1 handle SIGTERM?
a: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM first to allow a graceful shutdown (finish requests, close connections). If PID 1 ignores it, the pod waits out the grace period and is then killed with SIGKILL, dropping in-flight work.

q: What does the compiler's IR make possible?
a: One optimizer for many languages and many targets; front ends and back ends can be mixed (LLVM).

q: What does U puts in nm output mean?
a: The object file uses puts but doesn't define it; the linker (or loader) must find it, here in libc.

q: Why are Go binaries popular for FROM scratch images?
a: With CGO_ENABLED=0 they're statically linked: no libc or loader needed, only the kernel.

q: A security fix lands in OpenSSL. What's the difference for statically vs dynamically linked apps?
a: Dynamic: update the shared library (base image) once. Static: every binary must be rebuilt and redeployed.

q: Why do reproducible builds matter for supply-chain security?
a: Anyone can rebuild from source and check the binary is bit-identical, proving nothing was injected during the build.

q: What's the difference between ELF segments and sections?
a: Segments describe what the loader maps into memory and with which permissions; sections are for the linker, debuggers and tools and can be stripped.

q: Is main the first code that runs in a C program?
a: No. ld.so runs first (for dynamic binaries), then _start → __libc_start_main and constructors, then main.

q: A container fails with exec /app: no such file or directory but /app exists. Why?
a: Its interpreter (PT_INTERP, e.g. glibc's ld-linux) isn't in the image, or it's built for another architecture.

q: What is ASLR and why does it need PIE?
a: Randomizing where code, heap, stack and libraries load each run; the executable itself can only move if it's position-independent.

q: What does full RELRO protect?
a: It resolves all symbols at start and makes the GOT read-only, so an attacker can't overwrite function pointers in it.

page: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
q: Why are JVM services slow for the first minute after a deploy?
a: Code starts interpreted; the JIT compiles hot methods only after profiling them (warm-up).

page: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
q: Why doesn't adding threads speed up CPU-bound pure-Python code?
a: The GIL lets only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time (except in the free-threaded build).

page: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
q: A Node.js pod has a 4-CPU limit but never goes above 1 CPU. Why?
a: JavaScript runs on one thread; use worker threads or more, smaller replicas.

page: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
q: What should GOMEMLIMIT be set to in a container with a 1 GiB limit, and why?
a: Around 900 MiB: the GC then works harder before reaching the limit, avoiding OOMKills, while leaving headroom for non-heap memory.

page: 4.3 — Language runtimes: JVM, V8, Python, Go
q: The JVM's default max heap is 25% of the container memory. What do you change?
a: Set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (e.g. 70–75%), leaving room for off-heap memory.

q: At which stage does printf get its real address?
a: Not in the compiler or assembler. Those leave an undefined symbol. With static linking the linker fills it in; with dynamic linking the dynamic linker resolves it at start-up (or lazily on first call).

q: What's the difference between fork() and execve()?
a: fork() creates a new process that is a copy of the current one. execve() replaces the current process's program with a new one (same PID, new memory). Starting a program = fork + execve.

q: Your image runs fine on your laptop but fails on the cluster with exec format error. Why?
a: The binary was built for a different CPU architecture, e.g. arm64 (Apple Silicon) vs amd64 nodes. Build multi-arch images (docker buildx --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64).

q: Why can a Go binary run in a FROM scratch image but a typical C program can't?
a: A static Go binary contains everything it needs and has no PT_INTERP. A dynamically linked C program needs ld-linux.so and libc.so.6, which a scratch image doesn't have.

q: What does a JIT compiler do?
a: It watches which code runs often ("hot") and compiles that bytecode into native machine code while the program is running, so those parts run at near-native speed.

q: What does a switch do with a frame whose destination MAC it hasn't learned?
a: It floods it to all ports in that VLAN except the one it came in on.

q: You ping 8.8.8.8. Whose MAC address does your laptop ARP for?
a: The default gateway's; MACs only matter on the local link.

q: Why do VXLAN overlays usually need a smaller MTU?
a: VXLAN encapsulation adds ~50 bytes of headers; inner packets must shrink so the outer packet still fits in 1500.

q: Why doesn't gratuitous-ARP failover usually work in AWS/GCP VPCs?
a: The cloud network isn't a real L2 segment; the SDN controls which IP belongs to which interface and ignores GARP.

q: What problem does STP solve?
a: It blocks redundant links so broadcasts can't loop forever and cause a broadcast storm.

q: How many addresses are in a /22, and what range does 10.1.4.0/22 cover?
A host has routes for 10.0.0.0/8 via A and 10.0.5.0/24 via B. Where does 10.0.5.20 go?
a: Via B: the /24 is the longest matching prefix.

q: Do the source and destination IPs change as a packet crosses routers?
a: No (without NAT). Only TTL/checksum and the L2 (MAC) header change at each hop.

q: Why can blocking all ICMP break HTTPS for some users?
a: PMTU discovery depends on ICMP "fragmentation needed"; without it, big packets are dropped silently and connections hang.

q: Why must pod CIDRs not overlap with your corporate network?
a: Routes would be ambiguous: traffic to corporate IPs would be sent into the cluster (or vice versa) and peering/VPN can't be set up.

q: Why does a stateful firewall need only one rule for HTTPS while a NACL needs two?
a: conntrack lets replies of an allowed flow through automatically; a stateless NACL must explicitly allow the return traffic to ephemeral ports.

q: How does a packet to a ClusterIP reach a pod when no interface has that IP?
a: kube-proxy rules DNAT the destination to a chosen pod IP in PREROUTING/OUTPUT; conntrack keeps the mapping for the connection.

q: Many pods call one external API through a NAT gateway and get random connection timeouts. Likely cause?
a: SNAT source-port exhaustion to that single destination IP:port. Add NAT IPs, reuse connections, or spread destinations.

q: What happens to other traffic once a NetworkPolicy selects a pod for ingress?
a: All ingress not explicitly allowed by some policy is denied for that pod.

q: Why does externalTrafficPolicy: Local preserve the client IP?
a: Traffic only goes to pods on the node that received it, so no SNAT to another node is needed.

q: What makes a subnet 'public'?
a: Its route table has a default route to an internet gateway (and instances have public IPs).

q: Instances in a private subnet can't download packages. What do you check?
a: The subnet's route table has 0.0.0.0/0 → a NAT gateway in a public subnet, the NAT gateway is healthy, and SG/NACL allow outbound + return traffic.

q: VPC A is peered with B, and B with C. Can A reach C?
a: No. Peering isn't transitive; use a transit gateway or peer A and C directly.

q: Why is it better to reference security groups than CIDRs in rules?
a: Rules follow roles, not IPs: any instance (or pod with SG-for-pods) in the app SG is allowed, even as IPs change with autoscaling.

q: Your NAT gateway bill is huge. What's a common fix?
a: Add VPC endpoints for S3/ECR/other AWS services so that traffic bypasses the NAT gateway.

q: A packet goes through 12 routers. How many times does the destination IP change? And the destination MAC?
a: The destination IP stays the same the whole way (ignoring NAT on the server side). The destination MAC changes at every hop, because each L2 frame only goes to the next device.

q: Your laptop wants to reach 192.168.1.50 and 8.8.8.8. Which MAC address does it put on each frame?
a: For 192.168.1.50 (same /24): that machine's own MAC, found via ARP. For 8.8.8.8 (outside the subnet): the gateway's MAC.

q: What does a switch look at, and what does a router look at?
a: A switch looks at MAC addresses (L2). A router looks at IP addresses (L3) and its routing table.

q: Why can't a server on the internet open a connection to your laptop at home?
a: Your laptop only has a private IP behind NAT. The router only knows where to send incoming packets for conversations your side started (conntrack entries). Unsolicited inbound traffic has no mapping, unless you configure port forwarding.

q: What is the AWS equivalent of your home router's NAT?
a: A NAT gateway: instances in a private subnet send outbound traffic through it, and it rewrites their private IPs to a public one.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What does Cache-Control: no-cache actually mean?
a: The response may be stored, but it must be revalidated with the server (e.g. If-None-Match) before each use. To forbid storing, use no-store.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Your API works with curl but the browser shows a CORS error. Why, and where is the fix?
a: CORS is enforced only by browsers. The API (or the ingress in front of it) must return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for that origin, and answer the OPTIONS preflight with the allowed methods and headers.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Behind your load balancer every log line shows the same client IP. What's wrong?
a: The app logs the TCP peer (the LB). Read the client IP from X-Forwarded-For / Forwarded, and trust only entries added by your own proxies.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why must a CDN see Vary: Accept-Encoding?
a: The same URL exists in several encodings (br, gzip, none). Without Vary the CDN may serve a brotli body to a client that can't decode it.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Which cookie attributes stop JavaScript from reading a session cookie and stop it being sent over HTTP?
a: HttpOnly (no JS access) and Secure (HTTPS only). Add SameSite=Lax or Strict against CSRF.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Who actually walks the root → TLD → authoritative chain: your laptop or the resolver?
a: The recursive resolver. Your laptop's stub resolver sends one query and gets the final answer.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: You changed an A record with TTL 3600 ten minutes ago. Why do some users still see the old IP?
a: Resolvers that cached it before the change keep it until their copy's TTL expires (up to an hour), and some apps cache even longer.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why can a pod's lookup of api.stripe.com be slow, and what are two fixes?
a: ndots:5 makes it try every search suffix first, each for A and AAAA. Use the FQDN with a trailing dot, lower ndots, and/or run NodeLocal DNSCache.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What does DNSSEC protect against, and what doesn't it protect?
a: Forged or modified answers (authenticity and integrity). It doesn't hide which names you look up; that's DoH/DoT.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What is a subdomain takeover?
a: A CNAME still points at a cloud resource (bucket, app, CDN) that was deleted. An attacker claims that resource name and now serves content on your subdomain.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why does TCP need a handshake before sending data?
a: Both sides must agree on starting sequence numbers and confirm the other side is reachable and willing.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What's the difference between flow control and congestion control?
a: Flow control protects the receiver (rwnd, its buffer). Congestion control protects the network (cwnd, estimated from loss or bandwidth/RTT).

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Your service has 20,000 sockets in CLOSE_WAIT. What do you fix?
a: The application: it receives the peer's FIN but never closes its socket (leaked connections, missing close() / response body not closed).

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why do you get intermittent 502s when the LB idle timeout is 60 s and the backend's keep-alive timeout is 30 s?
a: The backend closes idle connections first; the LB may send a new request on a connection the backend just closed. Make the backend's timeout longer than the LB's.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why can one gRPC client overload a single pod behind a Kubernetes Service?
a: kube-proxy balances per TCP connection, and gRPC sends all requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection. Use L7 load balancing (mesh, gateway) or client-side balancing.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why doesn't TLS just use RSA/ECDSA to encrypt all the data?
a: Asymmetric crypto is slow. It's used once to agree keys and prove identity; the data uses fast symmetric ciphers.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What does the CertificateVerify signature prove that the certificate alone doesn't?
a: That the server has the private key. Anyone can copy a public certificate; only the owner can sign with its key.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Your site works in Chrome but curl says 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. Why?
a: The server isn't sending the intermediate certificate. Chrome had it cached; curl didn't. Serve the full chain.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why is the industry moving to 47-day certificates?
a: Revocation doesn't work reliably, so short lifetimes limit how long a stolen or mis-issued certificate is useful, and force automation.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Which ACME challenge do you need for .example.com?
a: DNS-01: wildcard certificates require a TXT record under _acme-challenge.example.com.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: HTTP/2 multiplexes streams. Why can it still suffer from head-of-line blocking?
a: Streams share one TCP connection; a lost TCP segment blocks delivery of all later bytes, so every stream waits.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: How does a browser find out a site supports HTTP/3?
a: Alt-Svc: h3=":443" on an earlier response, or an HTTPS DNS record. Then it tries QUIC and falls back to TCP if UDP is blocked.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why is 0-RTT data restricted to safe requests?
a: An attacker can replay the first flight. Replaying a GET is harmless; replaying a payment POST is not.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Your gRPC service behind a Kubernetes Service has one hot pod. Why?
a: gRPC keeps one long-lived HTTP/2 connection; kube-proxy balances connections, not requests.

q: What happens to a QUIC connection when the phone switches from Wi-Fi to 5G?
a: The IP changes but the Connection ID doesn't, so the connection migrates instead of reconnecting.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Which methods can a proxy safely retry automatically, and why?
a: Idempotent ones (GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE, OPTIONS): repeating them doesn't change the result. POST may create a duplicate.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: What's the difference between 401 and 403?
a: 401: we don't know who you are (missing/invalid credentials). 403: we know who you are and you're not allowed.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Users get 504 on a report endpoint that takes 90 s. Where do you look first?
a: The proxy/ingress/LB read timeout (often 60 s). Raise it for that route, or make the endpoint asynchronous (202 + polling).

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why do LLM chat UIs often use SSE rather than WebSockets?
a: The stream is one-directional (server → client), SSE is plain HTTP, works through proxies and CDNs, and reconnects automatically.

chTitle: Chapter 6 — Reaching the internet: DNS, TCP, TLS, HTTP
q: Why does gRPC return HTTP 200 even when the call failed?
a: gRPC reports its own status in the grpc-status trailer at the end of the stream; HTTP status only says the transport worked.

q: Your recursive resolver already knows .com's servers. Does it still ask the root for example.com?
a: No. It caches the root's referral (the .com NS records) for their TTL and goes straight to the .com servers. The root is only asked when that cache has expired.

q: Why does a new HTTPS request cost at least 2 RTTs before any HTTP data flows (TLS 1.3 over TCP)?
a: 1 RTT for the TCP handshake, then 1 RTT for the TLS 1.3 handshake. Only then can the HTTP request be sent. HTTP/3 merges the transport and TLS handshakes to save one of them.

a: The server sends a certificate for example.com signed by a CA the browser trusts, and proves it holds the matching private key (CertificateVerify). The browser checks the chain, the hostname and the validity dates.

q: 502 vs 504 from your load balancer: what's the difference?
a: 502 Bad Gateway: the LB got an invalid or no response from the backend (crashed, connection refused). 504 Gateway Timeout: the backend didn't answer in time.

q: Why can an L4 load balancer leave gRPC traffic unbalanced?
a: It balances connections; gRPC multiplexes all requests over one long-lived HTTP/2 connection, so one backend gets everything from that client.

q: What's the difference between readiness and liveness probes?
a: Readiness: should this pod receive traffic now? Liveness: is it stuck and should be restarted?

q: Why is a deep liveness check (that queries the DB) dangerous?
a: A DB hiccup fails every pod's liveness and Kubernetes restarts them all at once, turning a blip into an outage.

q: When is consistent hashing useful?
a: When the same key should hit the same backend (cache locality, shards) and you want few keys to move when backends change.

q: Users see 502s for a few seconds during every rollout. What do you check?
a: Graceful shutdown: readiness turning false before exit, a preStop sleep so endpoints update, SIGTERM handling, and LB deregistration delay.

q: Why delete the key on write instead of updating it in cache-aside?
a: Concurrent writers can update the cache in the wrong order, leaving an old value; deleting makes the next read fetch the current one.

q: What is a cache stampede and how do you prevent it?
a: Many requests miss the same expired hot key at once and all hit the DB. Use request coalescing/locks, stale-while-revalidate or early refresh with jittered TTLs.

q: Your Redis is at 100% CPU on one core while others are idle. Possible causes?
a: A slow command (KEYS, huge sets, Lua) or a hot key; Redis executes commands on one thread.

q: When is write-behind acceptable?
a: When losing the last few writes is tolerable (counters, metrics) and write speed matters more than durability.

q: What happens to the database when the cache cluster restarts empty, and how do you prepare?
a: It gets the full read load (cold cache). Warm critical keys, ramp traffic, and protect the DB with rate limits/circuit breakers.

q: Why is the WAL written before the data pages?
a: So a committed transaction can always be recovered by replaying the log after a crash, while data pages can be flushed lazily.

q: Why doesn't replication replace backups?
a: It copies every change, including mistakes and malicious deletes, to replicas within seconds; you need point-in-time backups to go back.

q: A query filters on created_at but the only index is on (tenant_id, created_at). Will it be used efficiently?
a: Generally no: B-tree composite indexes are used left-to-right; without tenant_id in the filter it can't seek efficiently.

q: What's the trade-off between sync and async replication?
a: Sync: no data loss on failover but higher commit latency and availability coupling. Async: fast commits but possible loss of recent transactions and stale replica reads.

q: You scale your app from 10 to 100 pods and Postgres starts refusing connections. Why and what's the fix?
a: Each pod's pool opens N connections; total exceeds max_connections. Use a connection pooler (PgBouncer/RDS Proxy) and smaller per-pod pools.

q: Why must consumers be idempotent?
a: With at-least-once delivery, a crash between processing and ack causes redelivery; the handler must produce the same result twice.

q: You have a topic with 6 partitions and scale consumers to 10. What happens?
a: Only 6 consumers get partitions; 4 sit idle. Parallelism is capped by the partition count.

q: What's the problem with 'write to DB, then publish to Kafka' in application code?
a: The two aren't atomic: a crash or publish failure after the commit loses the event (or the reverse order publishes events for data that was rolled back). Use an outbox/CDC.

q: What does a growing consumer lag tell you, and what do you do?
a: Consumers process slower than producers write. Scale consumers (up to partitions), fix slow handlers, or add partitions.

q: Queue or log for 'replay the last 7 days of events into a new analytics service'?
a: A log (Kafka) with ≥ 7 days retention; a queue deletes messages once consumed.

q: Why should app servers be stateless?
a: So any instance can serve any request and any instance can be added or killed at any time. That enables horizontal scaling, rolling deploys and self-healing.

q: What's the difference between an L4 and an L7 load balancer?
a: L4 forwards TCP/UDP connections by IP and port without reading the content. L7 understands HTTP, so it can route by host, path or header, terminate TLS and retry individual requests.

q: A user updates their profile and then immediately sees the old version. What could cause this?
a: Replication lag (the read went to a replica that hasn't caught up yet) or a stale cache entry that wasn't invalidated on write.

q: Why should queue workers be idempotent?
a: Most queues deliver "at least once", so a job can run twice (e.g. a worker crashes after doing the work but before acknowledging it). Running it twice must not charge a card twice.

q: Your API calls a payment provider that sometimes takes 30 s. What do you add?
a: A timeout on the call, retries with backoff (only if the call is idempotent), a circuit breaker, and ideally moving it to an async job so the user's request doesn't wait.

q: Why is CSS render-blocking but images aren't?
a: Without the CSSOM the browser can't know how anything looks or where it goes; painting without it would flash unstyled content. Images can fill in later.

q: What's the difference between defer and async?
a: Both download in parallel. defer runs after HTML parsing, in document order; async runs as soon as it's downloaded, in any order.

q: Why animate transform instead of left?
a: left triggers layout and paint every frame; transform can be handled by the compositor on the GPU without layout.

q: What is layout thrashing?
a: Interleaving DOM writes and layout reads so the browser must recompute layout synchronously many times per frame.

q: What can the infrastructure team do for rendering speed?
a: Lower TTFB (CDN, caching, streaming), compression, HTTP/2-3, early hints, correct cache headers and image optimization at the edge.

q: In what order do setTimeout(f,0), Promise.resolve().then(g) and a sync console.log run?
a: Sync log first, then g (microtask), then f (task).

q: Why does a 500 ms loop make clicks feel ignored?
a: The click handler is a task that can only run after the current task finishes; rendering also waits.

q: Does await block the main thread?
a: No. It pauses that async function and returns control to the event loop; CPU-bound code still blocks.

q: When should you use a Web Worker?
a: For CPU-heavy work (parsing, image/crypto processing, search) that would otherwise create long tasks on the main thread.

q: What's the server-side equivalent of a long task, and how do you detect it?
a: A blocking operation on the Node.js event loop; detect with event loop delay/utilization metrics.

q: Why can't Lighthouse report INP, and what does it show instead?
a: INP needs real user interactions over the page's life; Lighthouse shows Total Blocking Time as a lab proxy.

q: LCP is 4 s but TTFB is 3 s. Where do you start?
a: Server side: caching HTML at the CDN, backend/database latency, redirects, origin distance. The frontend can't fix a 3 s TTFB.

q: What does 'p75 LCP = 2.3 s' mean?
a: 75% of real page loads had LCP at or below 2.3 s; the slowest 25% were worse.

q: A cookie banner pushes the page down after load. Which metric suffers and how do you fix it?
a: CLS. Reserve its space from the start, overlay it, or show it without moving existing content.

q: Name three infrastructure changes that improve Core Web Vitals.
a: CDN caching of HTML/assets, HTTP/3 + Brotli compression, image optimization at the edge (also: Early Hints, removing redirect chains).

q: What exactly does the same-origin policy prevent?
a: Reading responses, DOM, cookies and storage of another origin; it doesn't prevent sending requests to it.

q: Why is XSS so dangerous even with the SOP in place?
a: The attacker's script runs on your origin, so the SOP treats it as your code: it can read pages and call APIs as the user.

q: How does SameSite=Lax stop most CSRF?
a: Cookies aren't attached to cross-site POSTs or subrequests, so a forged form submission from another site arrives without the session.

q: Is CORS a security feature that protects your API?
a: No. It's a controlled relaxation of the SOP for browser reads; it doesn't stop non-browser clients and isn't authentication.

q: Why roll out CSP in Report-Only mode first?
a: To see what legitimate scripts/styles would be blocked before enforcing, avoiding breaking the site.

q: Why can a plain <script src> in the <head> delay the whole page?
a: It's parser-blocking: the HTML parser stops, waits for the script to download and execute, and only then continues building the DOM. defer or async avoids this.

q: Which is cheaper to animate, left or transform: translateX()? Why?
a: transform. Changing left triggers layout and paint on the main thread every frame. transform can be handled by the compositor on the GPU without layout or paint.

q: A button click takes 400 ms to show any effect. Which metric gets worse, and what's the usual cause?
a: INP (Interaction to Next Paint). Usually a long JavaScript task on the main thread that blocks the event handler or the next rendering step.

q: What's the difference between View Source and the Elements panel?
a: View Source shows the original HTML bytes the server sent. Elements shows the current DOM, after the parser fixed things up and JavaScript changed it.

q: Why does each site get its own renderer process?
a: Security and stability. A compromised or crashing page is isolated in its own sandboxed process (Site Isolation) and can't read other sites' memory or bring them down.

q: Why does changing one line of source code rebuild npm install in a badly ordered Dockerfile?
a: The COPY . . comes before the install step; any source change invalidates that layer and every layer after it.

q: You RUN rm secret.key in a later step. Is the secret gone from the image?
a: No. It's still in the earlier layer; anyone with the image can extract it. Use build secrets.

q: What's the difference between a tag and a digest?
a: A tag is a movable name; a digest is a content hash that always identifies the same image bytes.

q: Which component actually calls clone() to create the container's namespaces?
a: runc (or another OCI runtime), started by containerd's shim on behalf of the kubelet.

q: Pods take 2 minutes to start on new nodes. Where do you look?
a: Image pull time: image size, registry throttling/latency, no cache on fresh nodes; use smaller images, mirrors, pre-pulling or lazy pulling.

q: Which component writes to etcd?
a: Only the API server; everything else reads and writes through it.

q: A pod stays Pending forever. What do you check?
a: kubectl describe pod events: insufficient CPU/memory requests, untolerated taints, unsatisfiable affinity, unbound PVC or zone mismatch.

q: Why did a pod you deleted come back?
a: Its ReplicaSet controller saw fewer pods than desired and created a replacement.

q: What does the scheduler use to decide if a pod fits: requests or actual usage?
a: Requests.

q: What's an operator?
a: A controller plus CRDs that automate running a specific application (create, scale, backup, upgrade, failover) the way a human operator would.

q: What are the three rules of the Kubernetes network model?
a: Every pod gets its own IP; pods can reach all other pods without NAT; agents on a node can reach all pods on that node.

q: What does the CNI plugin do when a pod starts?
a: Creates the pod's interface (veth), assigns an IP, sets routes, and makes the IP reachable from other nodes.

q: A Service exists but curl to it times out. First thing to check?
a: Its EndpointSlice: if empty, the selector doesn't match or no pods are Ready.

q: Why prefer Gateway API over Ingress for new setups?
a: It's the maintained standard with richer, portable features (traffic splitting, header matching, role separation), and the community ingress-nginx controller has been retired.

q: After applying a default-deny NetworkPolicy, nothing can resolve DNS. Why?
a: Egress to kube-dns (port 53) is now denied too; add an explicit allow rule for DNS.

q: Why 'build once, promote everywhere' instead of rebuilding per environment?
a: So production runs exactly the bytes that were tested; rebuilding can pull different dependencies or base images.

q: What's the main security advantage of pull-based GitOps?
a: CI doesn't need cluster credentials; the cluster pulls from git and only needs read access.

q: Someone runs kubectl edit in production. What does Argo CD with selfHeal do?
a: It detects drift from git and reverts the live object to the git state.

q: When is blue-green better than canary?
a: When you need an instant, all-at-once switch and instant rollback, and can afford double capacity briefly (or can't split traffic finely).

q: Why must DB migrations be backward compatible during rolling or canary deploys?
a: Old and new app versions run simultaneously against the same database.

q: Why shouldn't you use user_id as a Prometheus label?
a: Each distinct value creates a new time series; millions of users = millions of series, exploding memory, storage and query cost.

q: What's the difference between an SLI and an SLO?
a: The SLI is the measurement (ratio of good events); the SLO is the target for it over a time window.

q: Your SLO is 99.9% over 30 days. How much full downtime does the error budget allow?
a: 0.1% of 30 days ≈ 43.2 minutes.

q: Why alert on burn rate instead of 'error rate > 1% for 5 minutes'?
a: Burn rate ties alerts to the budget and user impact: fast burns page quickly, slow burns open tickets, and brief harmless blips don't wake anyone.

q: What does tail-based sampling give you that head-based sampling doesn't?
a: The decision is made after the trace completes, so you can keep all errors and slow traces while dropping most normal ones.

q: Is a container a small virtual machine?
a: No. It's a normal Linux process sharing the host kernel, isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups. A VM runs its own kernel on a hypervisor.

q: A pod is stuck in Pending. Which component hasn't done its job yet, and why might that be?
a: The scheduler hasn't bound it to a node, usually because no node has enough free CPU/memory for its requests, or because of taints, affinity rules or an unbound PersistentVolumeClaim. kubectl describe pod shows the reason in the events.

q: You delete a pod that belongs to a Deployment and a new one appears. Who created it?
a: The ReplicaSet controller (in kube-controller-manager). It saw actual replicas < desired replicas and created a new Pod object, which the scheduler and kubelet then made real.

q: What's the difference between push-based CD and GitOps?
a: In push-based CD the pipeline runs kubectl apply/helm upgrade against the cluster with cluster credentials. In GitOps an agent inside the cluster (Argo CD, Flux) pulls the desired state from git and reconciles continuously, so git is the source of truth and drift is corrected.

q: Your service is slow but CPU and memory look fine. Which signal do you reach for?
a: Traces, to see which downstream call or span is taking the time across services. Then logs for that specific request.

q: Why is everything in LLM infrastructure measured in tokens?
a: The model processes tokens, not characters or words. Compute per request, latency per step, KV cache memory and API cost all scale with the number of input and output tokens.

q: A MoE model has 120B total parameters but only 5B active per token. What do you size memory and compute for?
a: Memory for all 120B (every expert must be loaded), compute for roughly 5B per token. That's why MoE models are cheap to run per token but still need lots of GPU memory.

q: Why can past keys and values be cached in a decoder-only model?
a: Each token only attends to earlier tokens, and earlier tokens never change once generated. So their K and V vectors stay valid and can be reused for every following step.

q: What does temperature 0 mean?
a: Greedy decoding: always pick the most likely next token. Output becomes deterministic (given the same inputs and setup).

q: What's the difference between fine-tuning with LoRA and full fine-tuning, from an infra point of view?
a: LoRA trains small adapter matrices while the base weights stay frozen, so it needs far less GPU memory and produces small files. Many LoRA adapters can even be served on top of one shared base model.

q: Why are LLMs usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than FLOPS during decode?
a: Each decode step reads every weight once but only does ~2 FLOPs per weight per sequence. That's far below the ~300 FLOPs/byte the GPU needs to be compute-bound, so it waits on HBM.

q: What's the theoretical max decode speed of a 70B FP8 model on one GPU with 4.8 TB/s?
a: 70 GB of weights ÷ 4.8 TB/s ≈ 15 ms per token → ~70 tokens/s for a single stream (ignoring KV cache reads). Batching raises total throughput, not single-stream speed.

q: What's the difference between NVLink and InfiniBand?
a: NVLink is the scale-up link between GPUs inside a server or rack (TB/s, memory-like). InfiniBand (or RoCE) is the scale-out network between servers (hundreds of Gb/s per NIC).

q: What does GPUDirect RDMA save?
a: Copies through the CPU and system RAM. The NIC reads from and writes to GPU memory directly, which lowers latency and frees the CPU.

q: Why does every GPU get its own NIC in an AI server?
a: Collective operations (like all-reduce) make all GPUs send data at the same time. One NIC per GPU, each on its own "rail", gives every GPU full network bandwidth without sharing.

q: Your pod fails with \"CUDA driver version is insufficient for CUDA runtime version\". Where is the problem?
a: The host's driver is older than the CUDA runtime inside the image needs. Either upgrade the node driver (GPU Operator / node image) or use an image built for an older CUDA version.

q: Why doesn't a CUDA container image contain the GPU driver?
a: The driver includes a kernel module (nvidia.ko) that must match the host kernel and is loaded on the host. The toolkit mounts the matching user-space part (libcuda.so) from the host into the container at start-up.

q: When would you choose MIG over time-slicing?
a: When workloads from different teams or tenants share a GPU and need guaranteed memory and fault isolation with predictable performance. Time-slicing gives no isolation and no memory limits.

q: nvidia-smi shows 100% utilization but throughput is low. What do you check?
a: DCGM metrics like SM activity, tensor pipe activity and memory bandwidth. 100% "utilization" only means some kernel was running in the sample period; it may be tiny, memory-bound or waiting.

q: What does NCCL do, and on which hardware paths?
a: It implements collective communication (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter…) between GPUs, choosing NVLink/NVSwitch inside a node and InfiniBand/RoCE with GPUDirect RDMA between nodes.

q: Why is tensor parallelism usually kept inside one server (or NVLink domain)?
a: TP exchanges partial results in every layer, forward and backward. That needs the TB/s bandwidth and low latency of NVLink; over the network it would make every step wait.

q: Roughly how much memory does full training state need for a 13B model with AdamW and mixed precision?
a: About 16 bytes per parameter → ~208 GB, before activations. That's more than one GPU, so you'd use FSDP/ZeRO across several GPUs.

q: What is gang scheduling and why does distributed training need it?
a: Starting all processes of a job together or not at all. If only some ranks start, they block waiting for the others while holding expensive GPUs, and two such jobs can deadlock the cluster.

q: One node in a 512-GPU job has a slow NIC. What happens to the whole job?
a: Every collective waits for the slowest participant, so every step slows down to that node's speed. Straggler detection and replacing the node matter.

q: Your 1,000-GPU run checkpoints every 3 hours and a node fails every 4 hours on average. Why is that bad?
a: Each failure loses up to 3 hours × 1,000 GPUs of work plus restart time, and failures happen almost as often as checkpoints. Checkpoint more often (asynchronously) to raise goodput.

q: Users complain the first word takes 4 seconds to appear but then text flows fast. Which metric and which phase?
a: High TTFT: either queueing (not enough capacity, or bad routing) or slow prefill (very long prompts). Prefix caching, chunked prefill, more replicas or P/D disaggregation help.

q: Why does round-robin load balancing hurt LLM serving?
a: It ignores where each conversation's KV cache (prefix) lives, so requests keep landing on pods that must recompute the prefill. KV-aware routing sends them to the pod that already has the prefix.

q: How much KV cache does a 32-layer model with 8 KV heads of dimension 128 need for 100 concurrent 4k-token requests in BF16?
a: 2 × 32 × 8 × 128 × 2 bytes = 128 KB/token → × 4,096 tokens × 100 requests ≈ 54 GB.

q: Does speculative decoding change the model's answers?
a: No. Accepted tokens are exactly those the target model would have produced; the draft only lets several of them be confirmed in one forward pass.

q: Why split prefill and decode onto different GPUs?
a: They stress different resources (compute vs memory bandwidth). Mixed together, long prefills stall everyone's decode steps. Separate pools can be sized and scaled independently and tuned for their bottleneck.

q: What can DRA express that nvidia.com/gpu: 1 can't?
a: Attributes and relationships: a specific model or memory size, a MIG profile, several GPUs on the same NVLink domain, shared claims between pods. The device plugin only exposes a count.

q: A 64-GPU training job gets 40 pods scheduled and the rest stay Pending. What's wrong, and what fixes it?
a: No gang scheduling: the default scheduler placed pods one by one. The 40 running pods hold GPUs while waiting for the others. Kueue (or KAI/Volcano) admits the job only when all 64 GPUs are available.

q: Why should GPU nodes be tainted?
a: So that ordinary pods (web apps, sidecars, system jobs) don't land on very expensive GPU nodes and take CPU/memory that GPU workloads need. Only pods that tolerate the taint and request GPUs go there.

q: Your LLM Deployment scales up but new pods take 8 minutes to become Ready. What do you change?
a: Cache model weights close to the node (local NVMe pre-pull, shared PVC, OCI artifacts), use a streaming loader, keep a minimum number of warm replicas and scale earlier (on queue length rather than on SLO violations).

q: What does the endpoint picker in the Gateway API Inference Extension do that a normal Service doesn't?
a: It chooses a model server pod per request based on LLM-specific signals: prefix/KV cache locality, queue length, KV cache usage, LoRA adapters loaded. A Service just load-balances connections.

q: Why use hybrid search instead of vector search only?
a: Vectors capture meaning but are weak on exact tokens such as error codes, ticket IDs or product names. BM25 keyword search catches those. Combining both improves recall.

page: 10.7 — AI applications: RAG, agents, gateways, evals
q: Where should permissions be enforced in a RAG system?
a: At retrieval time: store ACL metadata with each chunk and filter the search by the user's identity, so the model never sees documents the user isn't allowed to read.

page: 10.7 — AI applications: RAG, agents, gateways, evals
q: What exactly does the model produce in tool calling, and who runs the tool?
a: The model produces a structured message naming the tool and its JSON arguments. The application (or its MCP client) validates and executes the call, then sends the result back to the model.

page: 10.7 — AI applications: RAG, agents, gateways, evals
q: What is prompt injection, and why is it a bigger risk for agents?
a: Instructions hidden in user input, documents or tool results that try to override the system's instructions. Agents act on systems with credentials, so a successful injection can cause real side effects, not just a bad answer.

page: 10.7 — AI applications: RAG, agents, gateways, evals
q: You change the system prompt to fix one complaint. How do you know you didn't break something else?
a: Run the eval suite (a versioned test set with graders) before and after the change, compare scores per category, and roll out gradually while sampling and grading live traffic.

q: Why is decoding usually limited by memory bandwidth rather than compute?
a: Each decode step produces one token per request, but it still has to read all model weights (and the KV cache) from HBM. There's little math per byte read, so the GPU waits for memory. Batching many requests together reuses each weight read for more tokens.

q: Can a 70B model in FP16 run on a single 80 GB GPU?
a: No. The weights alone are ~140 GB. Options: quantize (FP8 ≈ 70 GB, still tight with KV cache; INT4 ≈ 35 GB) or split the model across several GPUs with tensor parallelism.

q: What is the KV cache, and why does it limit concurrency?
a: It stores the attention keys and values of all previous tokens of each active request so they aren't recomputed every step. It grows with context length and the number of concurrent requests, and it has to fit in GPU memory next to the weights.

q: Why scale an LLM service on queue length or KV cache usage instead of CPU?
a: The work happens on the GPU. CPU usage stays low even when the GPU is saturated and requests are queuing, so CPU-based autoscaling would never react.

q: In RAG, what does the embedding model do, and what does the vector DB do?
a: The embedding model turns text (chunks and questions) into vectors that capture meaning. The vector DB stores the chunk vectors and quickly finds the ones closest to the question's vector, which are then added to the prompt.

q: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
a: Authentication proves who you are (login, token, certificate); authorization decides what that identity may do (roles, policies).

chTitle: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
page: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
q: Why is OIDC federation from CI to the cloud safer than storing an access key as a CI secret?
a: There's no long-lived secret to leak: each job gets a signed token describing exactly which repo/branch it is, exchanged for credentials that expire in about an hour and only for a scoped role.

chTitle: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
page: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
q: Are Kubernetes Secrets encrypted?
a: Only base64-encoded by default; anyone with RBAC get secrets can read them, and etcd stores them in plain text unless encryption at rest is configured.

chTitle: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
page: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
q: What does 'zero trust' change compared to a classic perimeter network?
a: Being inside the network grants nothing: every request is authenticated and authorized by identity, typically with mTLS and policies, so one compromised host can't reach everything.

chTitle: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
page: Chapter 11 — Security: identity, secrets, zero trust & supply chain
q: What does an SBOM help you answer during a new critical CVE?
a: Which of your images and services contain the affected package and version, so you know what to patch within minutes instead of days.

chTitle: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
page: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
q: Why can't you reliably tell a crashed node from a slow one?
a: Both look like "no answer yet". The only tool is a timeout, which is a guess; that's why systems must handle false failure detection.

chTitle: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
page: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
q: What does CAP force you to choose, and when?
a: During a network partition, either stay consistent (refuse some requests) or stay available (accept requests that may conflict). Without a partition, both are possible (but PACELC says consistency still costs latency).

chTitle: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
page: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
q: Why does etcd need a majority to commit a write?
a: Any two majorities overlap, so a committed entry is always known to at least one member of any future majority, which prevents two leaders committing conflicting histories.

chTitle: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
page: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
q: Why is a 4-member etcd cluster no better than 3 for failures?
a: Quorum of 4 is 3, so it still tolerates only 1 failure, while costing more and adding latency.

chTitle: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
page: Chapter 12 — Distributed systems: consensus, consistency & resilience
q: How does a retry storm happen, and how do you prevent it?
a: Multiple layers retry without backoff, multiplying load on a struggling dependency. Retry at one layer with exponential backoff, jitter and a retry budget, plus circuit breakers and load shedding.

chTitle: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
page: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
q: Why can a Kubernetes cluster be 'full' while CPU usage is 15%?
a: The scheduler packs by requests, not usage. If pods request far more than they use, nodes fill up on paper and the autoscaler adds nodes that stay mostly idle.

chTitle: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
page: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
q: When should you buy Savings Plans or committed use discounts?
a: For the steady baseline you are confident you'll run for 1–3 years, and only after right-sizing; otherwise you commit to paying for waste.

chTitle: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
page: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
q: Which workloads are good candidates for spot instances?
a: Stateless, fault-tolerant or retryable ones: web replicas behind a load balancer, batch jobs, CI runners, checkpointed training. Not single-instance databases.

chTitle: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
page: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
q: Why can traffic to S3 from private subnets be expensive, and how do you fix it?
a: Without a VPC endpoint it goes through the NAT gateway, which charges per GB processed. A gateway endpoint for S3 is free and keeps traffic private.

chTitle: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
page: Chapter 13 — Cloud cost (FinOps): where the money goes and how to keep it
q: What is unit economics and why does it matter more than the total bill?
a: Cost per business unit (per 1,000 requests, per customer). A growing bill can be healthy if unit cost falls; a flat bill can hide falling efficiency.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What does each part of m7g.xlarge mean?
a: m = general purpose family, 7 = generation, g = Graviton (ARM) processor, xlarge = size (4 vCPUs, 16 GiB for this family).

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why bake images instead of configuring servers after boot with SSH scripts?
a: Baked images are identical, tested and fast to boot; servers configured by hand drift into unique snowflakes that can't be reproduced or safely replaced.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: How does an Auto Scaling group heal a broken instance?
a: Health checks (instance status and load balancer checks) mark it unhealthy; the group terminates it and launches a replacement from the launch template to keep the desired count.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What is a cold start and how can you reduce it?
a: The delay when a new execution environment starts (runtime boot + initialization). Reduce it with small packages and fast runtimes, lazy initialization, provisioned/minimum instances or snapshot-based start.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: When are functions more expensive than containers?
a: For steady, high-traffic workloads: per-request and per-ms pricing adds up beyond the cost of always-on containers or VMs that serve many requests concurrently.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why can't an EBS volume attach to an instance in another availability zone?
a: Block volumes are replicated within a single AZ's storage network; to move data across zones you use snapshots (stored regionally) or application-level replication.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What's the difference between durability and availability for S3?
a: Durability is the probability your data isn't lost (11 nines); availability is the probability you can access it at a given moment (99.99% for Standard).

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What does a Multi-AZ database give you that a read replica doesn't?
a: A synchronous standby with automatic failover and no data loss; a read replica is asynchronous, used for read scaling, and may lag behind.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why do you need a connection pooler in front of PostgreSQL in Kubernetes?
a: Each connection is a backend process with memory cost; many pods with many connections can exhaust the database. A pooler multiplexes them onto fewer connections.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why must backups be copied to another account?
a: If attackers or a bad script get admin access to the production account, they can delete backups stored there; a separate, locked account preserves them.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why does Terraform need a state file?
a: To map each resource in code to the real object it created (IDs and attributes), so it can compute diffs, update and destroy the right things; the cloud API alone doesn't know which resources belong to your configuration.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What does -/+ in a plan mean and why is it dangerous?
a: Replacement: the resource will be destroyed and recreated because an immutable attribute changed. On stateful resources like databases or disks it means data loss or downtime.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why use remote state with locking?
a: So the whole team and CI share one source of truth, and two applies can't run at the same time and corrupt state.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: How do you bring a manually created bucket under Terraform management without recreating it?
a: Write the matching resource block and an import block (or terraform import), then run plan until it shows no changes.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What should a CI pipeline do on a Terraform pull request?
a: Format and validate, lint and policy/security scan, run plan and post it (plus cost diff) on the PR for review; apply only the reviewed plan after merge, using short-lived OIDC credentials.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why use separate accounts for prod and dev instead of one account with tags?
a: Accounts are hard isolation boundaries for IAM, quotas and blast radius; tags and naming conventions don't stop a dev-side mistake or compromised key from touching prod.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What can an SCP do that IAM policies in the account can't?
a: It sets a ceiling for everyone in the account, including its administrators, so rules like "never disable CloudTrail" or "only EU regions" can't be bypassed locally.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What's the difference between pilot light and warm standby?
a: Pilot light keeps data replicated and infrastructure ready but compute mostly off; warm standby runs a small working copy of the whole stack, so it recovers faster but costs more.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Which disasters are more common than a full region outage, and what protects against them?
a: Bad deployments, accidental deletes, data corruption and ransomware. Point-in-time recovery, versioning, and immutable backups in a separate account protect against them.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why run game days?
a: Untested DR plans fail on details (expired credentials, missing quotas, hard-coded endpoints); exercises reveal them and measure the real RTO and RPO.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
page: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What's the difference between a region and an availability zone?
a: A region is a geographic area with independent APIs and data; an availability zone is an isolated data center (or group) inside a region with its own power and network, close enough to the others for synchronous replication.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
page: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Under the shared responsibility model, who is responsible for a public S3 bucket leaking data?
a: The customer. The provider secures the infrastructure; configuration, access control and data are always the customer's responsibility.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
page: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why is 'multi-AZ' usually enough for high availability, and when do you need multi-region?
a: AZs have independent failure domains, so spreading across them survives data-center failures at low latency and cost. Multi-region is needed for regional outages, strict RTO/RPO, data residency or global latency, at much higher complexity.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
page: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: Why should production changes go through Infrastructure as Code instead of the console?
a: Code is reviewed, versioned, repeatable and can rebuild the environment after a disaster; console changes are invisible, unreproducible and drift from what everyone thinks exists.

chTitle: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
page: Chapter 14 — Cloud platforms: what you are really renting
q: What do RPO and RTO mean?
a: RPO is how much data (time) you can afford to lose; RTO is how long the service can be unavailable. Together they decide the backup and DR strategy and its cost.
